Let \(D_k=Q_k-P_k\) and put \(D_{-1}=D_{N-1}=0\), where the last equality follows from normalization. The set of compatible edge indices is \(\{i:0\le i<N-1,\ D_k=0\text{ for every }k\ne i,\ 0\le k<N-1\}\). Indeed, a gate on \((i,i+1)\) fixes every other amplitude and preserves \(x_i^2+x_{i+1}^2\). A prefix ending before \(i\) excludes both sites. A prefix ending after \(i\) includes both. Only the cut at \(i\) can change.

Conversely, if all differences away from cut \(i\) vanish, \(q_j-p_j=D_j-D_{j-1}\) shows that every outside population agrees and that \(q_i+q_{i+1}=p_i+p_{i+1}\). Write \((u,v)=(x_i,x_{i+1})\), \(U=\sqrt{q_i}\), \(V=\sqrt{q_{i+1}}\), and \(m=u^2+v^2=U^2+V^2\). If \(m>0\), take \(c=(uU+vV)/m\) and \(s=(uV-vU)/m\). Then \(c^2+s^2=1\) and \((cu-sv,su+cv)=(U,V)\). Choose \(\theta\) with \((\cos(\theta/2),\sin(\theta/2))=(c,s)\). This construction works independently for each signed input compatible with \(p\). If \(m=0\), both input and requested output pairs are zero, and any angle works on this pair when the outside reports agree.

When \(p=q\), all \(N-1\) locations work, even with angle zero. When \(p\ne q\), at least one \(D_k\) is nonzero by differencing. Exactly one such cut identifies its edge uniquely. Two or more such cuts exclude every single-gate explanation. A proposed pair initially carrying zero mass cannot account for any changed report.

The three prefix masses of \(p\) are \((1,3,4)/8\). For \(q^{(1)}\) they are \((1,2,4)/8\), so only edge \((1,2)\) fits. For example, with nonnegative input amplitudes on that pair one can take \(c=2\sqrt2/3,\ s=1/3\). For \(q^{(2)}\) the prefix masses are \((2,4,5)/8\), changing all three cuts. No single gate fits.

The unit target has nonempty support. Write \(L=\min(S\cup\{s\})\), \(R=\max(S\cup\{s\})\), and \(h=R-L\). If \(h>0\), the minimum is \(h\). If \(h=0\), the target is \(e_s\) or \(-e_s\). The former costs zero. The latter costs one for \(N\ge2\) and is unreachable for \(N=1\).

For each \(L\le k<R\), cut the path at the edge \((k,k+1)\). On the side not containing \(s\) there is at least one nonzero target coordinate: for \(k<s\) use \(L\), and for \(k\ge s\) use \(R\). That whole side is initially zero. Without a gate on the cut edge, it is acted on only by rotations internal to that side and therefore stays zero. Thus every circuit must use each of these \(h\) distinct edges. Excursions, repeat visits and cancellations preserve this lower bound.

For the upper bound, start with the target and root the interval \([L,R]\) at \(s\). Remove its leaves one at a time, keeping \(s\) to the end. On each leaf edge use one rotation to put the current pair norm at the parent and zero at the leaf; a zero pair needs at most the identity. This works in both edge orders: for the increasing-index pair \((u,v)\) of radius \(\rho>0\), coefficients \((c,b)=(u,-v)/\rho\) send it to \((\rho,0)\), while \((c,b)=(v,u)/\rho\) send it to \((0,\rho)\), with the block \(\begin{pmatrix}c&-b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\). Each removed coordinate then stays zero, regardless of the target signs or internal holes. There are \(h\) edges and no outside amplitudes. If \(h>0\), the last operation leaves a nonnegative root entry and orthogonality gives it norm one. Reverse the list and negate the angles to prepare the original signed target in at most \(h\) gates. The cut bound makes this optimal.

When \(h=0\), the empty circuit gives \(+e_s\), and it cannot give \(-e_s\). If \(N\ge2\), select either incident edge and set \(\theta=2\pi\), so the local block is \(-I_2\) and the neighboring zero remains zero. This witnesses the one-gate minimum. If \(N=1\) there is no edge, and only \(+e_s\) is reachable.

For the eight-site target, the interval is \([1,6]\), so the minimum is five. One explicit preparation from \(e_4\) uses the edges \((3,4),(2,3),(1,2),(4,5),(5,6)\) in that order. On the first choose \((\cos(\theta/2),\sin(\theta/2))=(4/5,3/5)\), then use \((0,-1)\) twice and \((0,1)\) twice. This sends \(-3/5\) to site \(1\) and \(4/5\) to site \(6\). For multisite \(S\) with extremes \(\ell<u\), the count is \(u-\ell+\operatorname{dist}(s,[\ell,u])\). Every site from \(\ell\) through \(u\) is optimal, including any holes, and each outside site costs strictly more.

Write \(w_v=a_v^2\). For a fixed schedule set \(I_0=\{r\}\) and obtain \(I_k\) from \(I_{k-1}\) by adding every neighbor paired in layer \(k\) with a vertex of \(I_{k-1}\). Thus a vertex is marked if its path from \(r\) has been traversed at strictly increasing layer times. A pair of zeros stays zero, and matching edges cannot relay through the same vertex twice in one layer. Induction gives \(\operatorname{supp}(y_k)\subseteq I_k\) for every choice of angles. Marks persist even if amplitudes cancel. Each \(I_k\) is connected. On a tree any newly marked vertex is entered from its unique parent, strictly after that parent was reached. Distinct children of one parent have distinct first-contact times.

For a schedule with \(I=I_d\), unit norm and Cauchy–Schwarz give \(|\sum_v a_vy_v|^2\le m_I:=\sum_{v\in I}w_v\). If \(m_I>0\), set \(b_v=a_v/\sqrt{m_I}\) on \(I\) and zero elsewhere. Retain the first-contact edge for each reached vertex other than the root, at its original layer. In reverse layer order, rotate each such signed pair to its positive pair norm at the parent and zero at the child. Use identities on the other edges. Each descendant is emptied before its parent, and the gates in any layer are disjoint. For \(|I|\ge2\), all amplitudes end at the root, whose last merge fixes its sign positive. Its norm is one. Inverting the rotations and reversing the order therefore prepares \(b\) in the original layers. For \(I=\{r\}\), \(e_r\) itself attains \(a_r^2\) even when \(a_r<0\). If \(m_I=0\), every supported output gives zero score and the empty circuit suffices. Thus maximizing \(m_I\) over marked sets gives exactly the best fidelity.

Define \(F(v,t)\) as the maximum marked weight in \(T_v\) in \(t\) further layers, starting with just \(v\) marked. For the child set \(C(v)\), take \(F(v,0)=w_v\) and, for \(t\ge1\), \[F(v,t)=w_v+\max_M\sum_{(u,j)\in M}F(u,t-j).\] Here \(M\) is any matching between \(C(v)\) and the time slots \(1,\ldots,t\), including the empty matching. An assigned pair \((u,j)\) schedules the first contact with \(u\) in slot \(j\). The answer is \(F(r,d)\).

For necessity, record the first contact time \(j\) for each reached child. The resulting child/time pairs form a matching. Actions within \(T_u\) before \(u\) is marked cannot spread any mark, and the layer that first reaches \(u\) cannot also relay through it. The marks below \(u\) therefore contribute at most \(F(u,t-j)\). Every reached vertex is counted once. For the converse, call matched children at their assigned times and start a maximizing subtree schedule for each in the next layer. Sibling subtrees are disjoint. The parent has at most one contact per layer, and the active interior of an earlier child does not touch the later parent contact. The union is a legal layer schedule and realizes exactly the sum. Subtree induction proves the recurrence. No restriction on revisiting edges was imposed on the circuits used in the upper bound.

Fill the table in postorder for budgets \(0,\ldots,d\). There are \(|V(T)|(d+1)\) entries. One entry uses a maximum-weight bipartite matching on at most \(|C(v)|+d\) vertices and \(|C(v)|d\) edges, plus ordinary sums. Polynomial-time matching gives polynomial total real operations and comparisons. Store the maximizing assignments to recover a contact schedule and use the signed rotations above. A leaf has \(F(v,t)=w_v\) at every budget. In particular a root-only tree has score one, and any tree at zero budget has score \(a_r^2\).

In the example the optimal scores at \(d=1,2,3\) are \(0,1/2,1\). One layer reaches neither grandchild. To reach a grandchild by layer two, the root must call its parent in layer one, when it can call only one child. Full-amplitude transfers along \(r,u,u'\) in two successive layers capture weight \(1/2\). At depth three use \((r,u)\), then simultaneously \((u,u')\) and \((r,v)\), then \((v,v')\). Let the first gate put \(1/\sqrt2\) at each of \(r,u\); the layer-two gates transfer these amplitudes positively to \(v,u'\). The last gate transfers the amplitude at \(v\) to \(v'\) with negative sign. This gives \(a\) exactly. The two grandchildren lie in the distance-two ball but their total weight one is unattainable at depth two.

For any input label \(x\), the first factor to act contributes \(a(x)\) and sends the ket to \(|p(x)\rangle\). The second gate acts on that label, so \(M(b,q)M(a,p)|x\rangle=a(x)b(p(x))|q(p(x))\rangle\). In an entrywise calculation the only possible intermediate row is \(p(x)\).

In the order \(D_fP_p\), the coefficient in column \(x\) at row \(p(x)\) is \(f(p(x))\). In \(P_pD_g\) it is \(g(x)\). Equality on this basis is equality of the operators, and it fixes the unique table \(g(x)=f(p(x))\). Keeping \(g=f\) gives exact equality if and only if \(f(p(x))=f(x)\) for all \(x\), equivalently \(f\) is constant on every cycle of \(p\).

Choose the orientation \(D_fP_p=\lambda P_pD_f\). As every \(f(x)\) has modulus one, this identity holds exactly when the ratios \(f(p(x))/f(x)\) have a common value \(\lambda\) on all of \(X\). Necessity follows by reading each column, and substituting the common value proves sufficiency. In the reverse identity the corresponding scalar is \(\overline{\lambda}\). A different scalar on each cycle does not in general give a single scalar for the operator.

In the two-bit example the input-side table is \(g(c,t)=e^{i\theta(t\oplus c)}\). For \(c=0\) the unchanged orders agree and the ratio is one. For \(c=1\) the ratios at \(t=0,1\) are \(e^{i\theta}\) and \(e^{-i\theta}\), respectively. Thus a common ratio must be one, and it exists precisely for \(\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z\). At every such angle both orders agree exactly. This gives the same set of angles for the two tests.

At \(\theta=\pi\), take \(|\psi\rangle=(|00\rangle+|10\rangle)/\sqrt2\) in control-first order. In \(D_fP_p|\psi\rangle\), the phase gate acts on \(|11\rangle\) after the target flips, giving \((|00\rangle-|11\rangle)/\sqrt2\). In \(P_pD_f|\psi\rangle\), both input targets are zero, giving \((|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2\). The inner product is \((1-1)/2=0\). For each individual basis input, both orders land with probability one on the same \(p(c,t)\), since their only nonzero coefficients have modulus one.

Put \(r_x=b_x/a_x\in\mathbb T\). Acting on \(|x\rangle\), the right side of \(U_b=DU_aD^\dagger\) has coefficient \(\overline{d_x}a_x d_{p(x)}\) at \(|p(x)\rangle\). Thus the operator equation is equivalent to \(d_{p(x)}=r_xd_x\) for every edge. For \(j\geq0\) write \(R(v,j)=\prod_{k=0}^{j-1}r_{p^k(v)}\), with \(R(v,0)=1\). Chaining the edge equations gives \(d_{p^j(v)}=R(v,j)d_v\).

On a cycle \(C\) of length \(L\), returning to a starting vertex gives \(\prod_{x\in C}r_x=1\). Equivalently \(\prod_{x\in C}a_x=\prod_{x\in C}b_x\) on this very cycle. A second necessary check is local to the references. For any two reference labels \(s,t\) on the same cycle take the unique \(0\leq j<L\) with \(p^j(s)=t\). The forward arc must satisfy \(\eta_t=R(s,j)\eta_s\). It suffices to use one reference as the base on each pinned cycle and to compare it with every other pin. With closure in force, this is equivalent to testing all reference pairs. With a single pin there is no additional pairwise condition.

These tests suffice. Pick one vertex \(v\) per cycle. On a pinned cycle choose \(v\in S\) with \(d_v=\eta_v\); otherwise choose any \(d_v\in\mathbb T\). Set \(d_{p^j(v)}=R(v,j)d_v\) for \(0\leq j<L\). All constructed values have modulus one. The recurrence checks each edge except the closing one. The full-cycle condition gives the final edge back to \(v\). The reference-arc tests give the other prescribed values. The resulting diagonal unitary therefore satisfies the exact matrix equation. Conversely the starting value determines every other phase in its cycle by the same recurrence. There is one free unit phase on each unpinned cycle and no freedom on a compatible pinned cycle. A fixed point requires \(a_x=b_x\); its phase is arbitrary if unpinned and equals \(\eta_x\) if pinned.

Without fixed references, the product is the complete invariant of a labeled cycle. Necessity is the telescoping product, and sufficiency is the construction with arbitrary starting phase on that cycle. In particular any unit edge weights with the same product are related this way. If desired, one representative places the entire product on the closing edge and gives weight one to the other edges.

For a concrete failure with references, use \(X=\{0,1\}\), \(p(0)=1\), \(p(1)=0\), \(a_0=a_1=1\), and \(b_0=b_1=-1\). Both devices have the product \(+1\) for the sole cycle. They are compatible without pins, for example with \((d_0,d_1)=(1,-1)\). Pin both labels at \(\eta_0=\eta_1=1\). The forward edge \(0\to1\) forces \(d_1=-d_0=-1\), in conflict with its prescribed value. The conflict persists despite exact matching of the closed product.

Induction on \(n\) gives \(U^n|x\rangle=(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}a_{p^j(x)})|p^n(x)\rangle\). On a cycle \(C\) of length \(\ell\), the basis vector returns to its label exactly when \(\ell\mid n\). In that case the product is \(h_C^{n/\ell}\) at each of its \(\ell\) starting points. At all other positive powers its diagonal entries vanish on this cycle. Hence \(t_n=\sum_{C:\,|C|\mid n}|C|h_C^{n/|C|}\).

Each orbit span is invariant, and these spans form a direct sum. For a representative \(v\) of an \(\ell\)-cycle, the vectors \(|v\rangle,U|v\rangle,\ldots,U^{\ell-1}|v\rangle\) are an orthonormal basis of that span, since they are unit phases times distinct basis vectors. The operator shifts these basis vectors, and sends the last to \(h_C|v\rangle\). The resulting companion matrix has characteristic polynomial \(z^\ell-h_C\). Equivalently, \(U^\ell=h_CI\) on that span and no smaller-degree monic polynomial annihilates the cyclic vector, so its degree-\(\ell\) minimal polynomial is its characteristic polynomial. Taking the product over the blocks yields \(\det(zI-U)=\prod_C(z^{|C|}-h_C)\). A fixed point gives \(z-a_x\).

For distinct cycle lengths let \(\mathcal L\) be the set of occurring lengths and let \(h_\ell\) denote the product of the unique \(\ell\)-cycle. Visit \(\mathcal L\) in increasing order. Evaluating the trace formula at \(n=\ell\) yields \[h_\ell=\frac{1}{\ell}\left(t_\ell-\sum_{\substack{d\in\mathcal L,\ d<\ell,\ d\mid\ell}} d\,h_d^{\ell/d}\right).\] The sum is empty at the smallest length. Every term subtracted at a later stage belongs to a shorter divisor and has already been identified; longer cycles cannot return. There is precisely one still-unknown term, and its coefficient \(\ell\) is nonzero. Since every length is at most \(N\), the supplied traces suffice. The known permutation assigns each recovered value to its particular cycle.

For an ambiguity take \(p=(1)(2)(3\,4)(5\,6)\) and list weights by input labels \(1,\ldots,6\). Use \(a=(1,-1,1,-1,1,1)\) and \(a'=(i,-i,1,1,1,1)\). In the first case the fixed-point products are \(\{1,-1\}\) and the transposition products are \(\{-1,1\}\). In the second they are \(\{i,-i\}\) and \(\{1,1\}\), respectively. Every edge has unit modulus. By the factor formula both characteristic polynomials are \((z^2-1)^2(z^2+1)\). The two fixed factors in the first assignment supply \(z^2-1\); those in the second supply \(z^2+1\). The same eigenvalue multiset gives the same trace of every positive power, since these unitaries are diagonalizable. Permuting same-length cycles cannot turn one of the displayed multisets into the other.

For a fixed length \(\ell\), form \(s_k=\operatorname{tr}(P_\ell U^{k\ell})/\ell\). Each length-\(\ell\) cycle returns at that power and other lengths are excluded by the projection, so \(s_k=\sum_{|C|=\ell}h_C^k\). Newton’s identities determine the monic polynomial \(\prod_{|C|=\ell}(w-h_C)\) from \(s_1,\ldots,s_{m_\ell}\). Concretely \(e_0=1\) and \(j e_j=\sum_{k=1}^{j}(-1)^{k-1} e_{j-k}s_k\) yield the elementary symmetric coefficients, with alternating signs in that polynomial. The roots give the product multiset with its multiplicities, even when some roots coincide.

These projected reports and the global traces are symmetric in the products of same-length cycles. Any permutation of those products is realizable on the known routing by placing its assigned product on one directed edge of each cycle and putting weight one on all remaining edges. Thus every assignment of the recovered multiset to that length’s labels is possible. The assignment is unique for that length exactly when all those products are equal, including a length occurring once. All labels are determined exactly when this condition holds for every occurring length.
